la:noun:ambulatiuncula.html:
ambŭlātĭuncŭla, ae,
dim. f. [ambulatio], a short walk (perh. only in the foll. passages of Cic.).
Lit., . —And,
Concr., a small place for walking: tecta,.

senses: a place for walking; promenade, walk, portico
la:noun:ambulatio.html:
ambŭlātĭo, ōnis, f.
id.
,
a walking about, a walk (only in prose, oftenest in Cic.).
Lit.: ambulationem pomeridianam conficere in Academiā,: compitaliciae,: ventum est in ambulationem,: recta, flexuosa,.—Of the orator on the platform: conveniet etiam ambulatio quaedam propter immodicas laudationum moras,.—Hence,
Transf., concr., a walk, a place for walking, a promenade (usu. near a dwelling; either covered or open): ambulatio sub dio pedes lata denos. ; so ; ; ; ; .

la:verb:ambulo.html:
ambŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n.
regarded by Doed. as a sort of dim. of ambio, but better regarded as comp. of am- and the root of βαίνω, beto, -bito, baculum = βάκπρον, vado, venio; Sanscr. gā = go; Germ. gehen; Engl. go. Curtius
.
Lit.
In gen., to go about, to walk: cum illā neque cubat neque ambulat,: si non ubi sedeas locus est, est ubi ambules,: quem ad modum quis ambulet, sedeat,: sedetur, ambulatur, Müll.: ambulatum est,; : cum sedeatur, ambuletur, discumbatur,: standi ambulandi vices,: ambulans aut jacens,; : cum ambulantis Tiberii genua advolveretur,: aves aliquae ambulant, ut cornices; aliae saliunt, ut passeres,walk,: Aegyptii mures bipedes ambulant,: claudi ambulant,; ; ; .—Hence,
Esp., to walk for recreation, to take a walk: abiit ambulatum,: visus sum mihi cum Galbā ambulare,: cum in sole ambulem, etiamsi aliam ob causam ambulem, etc.,: pedibus ambulare,.—
To go, to travel, to journey (class.), : quo ambulas tu?; : biduo aut triduo septingenta milia passuum ambulare,; : eo modo Caesar ambulat, ut, etc., et saep.—Hence, in the comic poets, bene ambula, farewell, a good journey to you, a form oft. used at the departure of any one: bene ambula et redambula,farewell and farewell back,: Ty. Bene ambulato. Ph. Bene vale, ; and absol.: ambula,go,: ambulare in jus, to go into court, go to law: ambula in jus,; .—
To walk about with a certain gravity or importance: licet superbus ambules pecuniā. ; ; .—
Of inanimate things: amnis, quā naves ambulant,: Nilus immenso longitudinis spatio ambulans,: velut intus ambulantem (lucem),.—Trop. (only post-Aug.): quod deinde caput translatum per omnes leges ambulavit,was afterwards added to all laws,; : ambulat cum domino bonorum possessio,.—
Act., esp. with cognate objects, as iter, via, etc., to navigate, sail, pass over, etc.: cum Xerxes tantis classibus tantisque copiis maria ambulavisset terramque navigāsset,: perpetuas ambulat illa vias, (cf.: ire iter, viam, etc., Burm. ad ).— Pass.: si bina stadia ambulentur,.—
In milit. lang. t. t., to march: ut ter in mense tam equites quam pedites educantur ambulatum,.—
In the jurists in opp. to ire: iter est jus eundi ambulandi hominis,of one going and coming,.—
Trop. very freq. in eccl. Lat. (like Heb. and N. T. Gr. περιπατέω), to walk, in the sense of to live, with an adjunct of manner or circumstances: ambulavit Henoch cum Deo,: ut ambules in viis ejus (Dei),: qui ambulant in lege Domini,: in circuitu impii ambulant,: fraudulenter ambulare, .—So also very freq. in N. T., but only once in this sense in the Gospels: quare discipuli tui non ambulant juxta traditionem seniorum?: qui non secundum carnem ambulant,: in carne ambulantes,: honeste ambulare,: ut ambuletis digne Deo,: quod non recte ambularent, et persaepe.

la:adj:ambitiosus.html:
ambĭtĭōsus, a, um, adj.
ambitio
.
(Very rare and mostly poet.) Going round, encompassing;poet., embracing, twining round: lascivis hederis ambitiosior, (cf.: undique ambientibus ramis,).—Of a river, making circuits, having many windings: Jordanes amnis ambitiosus,.— Of oratorical ornament, excessive, superfluous: vir bonus ambitiosa recidet Ornamenta,.—
Transf.
That asks for a thing fawningly; esp., that solicits the favor, good-will, etc., of any one, in a good and bad sense, honor-loving, ambitious, courting favor; vain, vainglorious, conceited, etc.: qui ita sit ambitiosus, ut omnes vos nosque cotidie persalutet,: homo minime ambitiosus, minime in rogando molestus,: ne forte me in Graecos tam ambitiosum factum esse mirere,desirous of the favor of the Greeks,: pro nostris ut sis ambitiosa malis, Ov P. 3, 1, 84: pro nato caerula mater Ambitiosa suo fuit,i.e. begs fawningly of Vulcan for weapons for her son,: malis artibus ambitiosus,seeking to ingratiate one's self,: salubris magis princeps quam ambitiosus,—
Pass., that is willingly solicited or entreated, ambitious; much sought, honored, admired: ambitiosus et qui ambit et qui ambitur,: turba caelestes ambitiosa sumus,: sexus muliebris saevus, ambitiosus, potestatis avidus,: si locuples hostis est, avari; si pauper, ambitiosi,: nota quidem sed non ambitiosa domus,not sought after, Jahn: ambitiosae pulchritudinis scortum. . —
Of things, vain, ostentatious: amicitiae,founded merely on the desire to please, interested,: rogationes,; so : gloriandi genus,: preces,urgent,: sententiae,: mors, ambitious, i. e. to obtain fame, : medicina ars,boastful,: et quaesitorum pelago terrāque ciborum Ambitiosa fames,: atria,splendid, gorgeous,: ambitiosis utilia praeferre,: ambitiosius id existimans quam domi suae majestas postularet,more condescending, submissive,.—
In rhet.: orator ambitiosus, who seeks to rouse attention by obsolete or unusual expressions: antigerio nemo nisi ambitiosus utetur,.—Hence, adv.: ambĭtĭōsē, ambitiously, ostentatiously, etc.: de triumpho ambitiose agere,: ambitiose regnum petere,: amicitias ambitiose colere, Tac.

H. 1, 10 al.—Comp., .—Sup., .

la:noun:ambitio.gloss: A going around or about; that which surrounds.
senses: A going around or about; that which surrounds.
A desire for one's favor or good will; excessive desire to please, flattery, adulation.
A desire for honor, popularity, power or display; ambition; vanity.
The going about of candidates for office in Rome, and the soliciting of citizens for their vote; candidature; canvassing.
la:noun:ambitio.html:
ambĭtĭo, ōnis, f.
ambio
,
a going round.
In the time of the republic, t. t. (v. ambio, II. B.), the going about of candidates for office in Rome, and the soliciting of individual citizens for their vote, a canvassing, suing for office (by just and lawful means; while ambitus denotes unlawful means, as bribery, threats, etc.): quid de nostris ambitionibus loquar?: mea me ambitio ab omni illā cogitatione abstrahebat,: cum ambitionis nostrae tempora postulabant,: si infinitus forensium rerum labor et ambitionis occupatio decursu honorum etiam aetatis flexu constitisset,: hic magistratus a populo summā ambitione contenditur,: tanta exarsit ambitio, ut primores civitatis prensarent homines, et saep.—
In gen., a striving for one's favor or good-will; an excessive desire to please, flattery, adulation: ambitione labi,: sive aliquā suspitione sive ambitione adducti,: in Scipione ambitio major, vita tristior, Heus., Beier, and Gernh.: Dionysius Platonem magnā ambitione Syracusas perduxit, in an ostentatious manner, for the purpose of securing his favor, Br. and Dähn.: ambitio (i.e. studium Fabiis placendi) obstabat,: ambitione relegatā,without flattery,: ambitionem scriptoris facile averseris, obtrectatio et livor pronis auribus accipiuntur, : nullo officii aut ambitionis genere omisso, i.e. nullis blanditiis,: coronas quam parcissime et sine ambitione tribuit, et saep.—Hence, also partiality: jus sibi per ambitionem dictum non esse,.—
With the predom. idea of the purpose or end, a desire for honor, popularity, power, display, etc.; in bon. part., ambition; in mal. part., vanity.—So in Lucr. of the ambitious efforts of men: Angustum per iter luctantes ambitionis,struggling to press through the narrow way of ambition,: me ambitio quaedam ad honorum studium duxit,: Miserrima omnino est ambitio honorumque contentio,: a quo incepto studioque me ambitio mala detinuerat,: aut ab avaritiā aut miserā ambitione laborat,: Vitā solutorum miserā ambitione gravique,; so ; 2, 6, 18: inanis,: levis,: licet ipsa vitium sit ambitio, tamen frequenter causa virtutum est,: perversa,: funerum nulla ambitio,no display, pomp,.—
Great exertion: cum admitti magnā ambitione aegre obtinuisset,.—
That which surrounds (v. ambio, 2.; postclass. for ambitus): vimineos alveos circumdant ambitione tergorum bubulorum,with a wrapping of cowhide,: fuliginem ambitio extimae cutis cohibet,: ita assedimus, ut me ex tribus medium lateris ambitione protegerent, Min. Oct. 4.

la:noun:ambages.gloss: an indirect, roundabout path; a wandering to and fro, twists and turns
senses: an indirect, roundabout path; a wandering to and fro, twists and turns
circumlocution, ambiguity, evasion, digression, beating about the bush
la:noun:ambages.html:
ambāges, is, f. (nom. and
gen. sing. dub., though mentioned in P. and found in MS.; but found in abl. sing.: ambage,; ; ; also, ambagine,; the plur. is complete, gen. ambagum, ; cf. Schne) [ambi-ago], a going round, a roundabout way (poet.; in prose only postAug.; syn.: ambago, sinus, flexus, circuitus).
Lit.: variarum ambage viarum (of the windings of the labyrinth), ; cf.: dolos tecti ambagesque resolvit,: (Luna) multiformi ambage torsit ingenia contemplantium,: itinerum ambages,: longis ambagibus,.—
Of speech.
Circumlocution,evasion, digression: ambages mitte,; so (not elsewh. in Plaut.): ambages mihi Narrare occipit, * : per ambages et longa exorsa tenere,; : ne te longis ambagibus morer,: missis ambagibus,without circumlocution, directly,; ; .—
Obscurity, ambiguity (as kindr. with ambiguus).—So of the Theban Sphinx: immemor ambagum,; .—Of the lang. of oracles: ambage nexa Arcana tegere,: eā ambage Chalcedonii monstrabantur,; .—Also transf. to actions: per ambages,in an obscure, enigmatical manner,; ; .

la:adj:ambrosius.html:
ambrŏsĭus, a, um, adj., = ἀμβρόσιος,
immortal, divine, ambrosial (syn.: immortalis, divinus), in gen., all that pertains to the gods, and their prerogatives and endowments; hence, an epithet for every thing lovely, pleasant, sweet, etc. (in gen. only poet.): comae,; so : dapes,: suci,; : sinus, 110: corpus,: pedes,, p. 258, 39: color,, p. 254, 4: nectar,.

la:noun:ambrosia.gloss: The food of the gods; ambrosia.
senses: The food of the gods; ambrosia.
The plant, artemisia, of the genus Artemisia.
la:noun:ambrosia.html:
ambrŏsĭa, ae, f., = ἀμβροσία.
Lit., ambrosia, the food of the gods (as nectar was their drink): non enim ambrosiā deos aut nectare laetari arbitror,; : Suaviolum dulci dulcius ambrosiā,.—Hence: orator ambrosiā alendus, prov. once in Cic., qs. agod among orators, of a distinguished orator (opp. faenum esse), .— Also food for the steeds of the gods: equos ambrosiae suco saturos,; (acc. to Hom. Il. 5, 368 and 369).—
Transf.
The unguent of the gods (so, ἀμβροσία, Hom. Il. 14, 170; 16, 670): ambrosiā cum dulci nectare mixtā Contigit os,: liquidum ambrosiae diffundit odorem,; .—
The name of several plants, esp. of the botrys or artemisia, Turkish mugwort: Choenopodium botrys, Linn.; .—Another plant of this name, .—
An antidote to poison, .

la:num:ambo.html:
ambō^, bae, bo,
num. (nom. plur. ambo for ambae, ; acc. plur. orig. ambo, analog. to the Gr. ἄμφω, but from the adj. use of the word ambos arose; acc. ambo is found in ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; Afran. ap. P.; Cic. (who never uses ambos) Fam. 5, 8; 9, 13; Caes. (who never uses ambos) B. C. 1, 48; Verg. (who never uses ambos) E. 6, 18; ; ; Hor. (who never uses ambos) S. 2, 3, 180; 2, 7, 62; ; ; ; 26, 26; 27, 27; 30, 14; 35, 22; 38, 53; 40, 46; 41, 18; 45, 19; ; Sil. 4, 175; 17, 427 al.; ambos is found in Rib. bis; ; ; Ter. (who never uses ambo) Eun. 5, 8, 39; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; Sall. (who never uses ambo) J. 21, 4; Kritz; Ov. (who never uses ambo) H. 10, 51; Tac. (who never uses ambo) A. 13, 54; ; ; cf. ; P.; Rudd. I. p. 57; Kühn. ad ; Neue, Formenl. II. p. 145 sqq.) [ἄμφω, ἀμφότεροι, Paul. ex Müll.; kindr. with Sanscr. ubhāu, dual nom. = ambo; Zend. uba; Slav. oba; Lith. abù; Goth. bai, bajōths; Germ. beide; Engl. both], both (of two objects whose duality is assumed as already known; when not already known, they are designated by duo. The difference between ambo and uterque is thus given by P.: Ambo non est dicendum, nisi de his, qui uno tempore quid faciunt, utpote reges Eteocles et Polynices ambo perierunt quasi unā; Romulus autem et Africanus non ambo triumphārunt, sed uterque; quia diverso tempore).
Of objects naturally in pairs, as the parts of the body, both: manusque ambas,; : ambas palmas,; 10, 844: tinnient ambae aures ejus,; : circum unum ambove genua, (but even here we find duo: sumes duos renes (vituli) et adipem,; : duas manus,bis; 18, 9: duae palmae manuum ejus,: duorum luminum,of both eyes,; so Shaksp., her two eyes, Love's Lab. Lost, iv. 3; Haml. i. 4).—So of other things: Tristior illā Terra sub ambobus non jacet ulla polis,: Atridas Priamumque, et saevum ambobus Achillen,angry with both parties,.—
In gen., of two objects and no more, the two, both: QVOM. PERORANT. AMBO. PRAESENTES. (i.e. actor et reus), Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. : consules, alter ambove, si eis videretur,: ambo accusandi estis,: jam hisce ambo, et servos et era, frustra sunt duo,: erroris ambo complebo,: emit hosce ambos,: ut eos ambos fallam,; so : hic, qui utrumque probat, ambobus debuit uti,: una salus ambobus erit,: plebiscitis cautum, ne quis duos magistratus uno anno gereret, utique liceret consules ambos plebeios creari,: Caesar atque Pompeius diversa sibi ambo consilia capiunt ... eodemque die uterque eorum ex castris exercitum educunt,: amborum verba,: civitate Romanā ambos donavit,: ambo occisi,: errant autem ambo senes,; : applicuit ambos ad eum,; .—
Poet. = duo: partīs ubi se via findit in ambas,into two,.

la:adj:ambiguus.gloss: going two ways, hither and thither, moving from side-to-side
senses: going two ways, hither and thither, moving from side-to-side
wavering, not to be relied on, untrustworthy, unreliable, treacherous
la:adj:ambiguus.html:
ambĭgŭus, a, um, adj.
ambigo
,
going about, hither and thither.
Lit.: per ambiguum favorem gratiam victoris spectare,i. e. in that they show equal friendliness to both sides,: ambiguus Proteus,who sometimes takes one form, sometimes another, changeable,: ambiguus fuerit, modo vir, modo femina, Scython,: Inque virum soliti vultus mutare ferinos Ambigui prosecta lupi,they sometimes assume the form of a wolf and sometimes that of a man,: promisit Ambiguam Salamina, h. l. = alteram,a second Salamis,. —
Transf.
Uncertain, doubtful (syn.: dubius, incertus): ambiguum est quod in ambas agi partes animo potest. Hujusmodi apud Graecos ἀμφίβολα dicuntur, Paul. ex Müll.: quidquid incerti mihi in animo prius aut ambiguom fuit, Nunc liquet, nunc defaecatum est,: etiam si dudum fuerat ambiguom hoc mihi, * : difficile et ambiguum,: haud ambiguus rex, i. e. sine dubio rex futurus,.—Subst.: ambĭgŭum, i, n., doubt, uncertainty: in ambiguo est,: in ambiguo relinquere,: non habui ambiguum, Brut. ap. : servet in ambiguo Juppiter,: non sane alias magis in ambiguo Britannia fuit,.—Also in acc. absol. in the Gr. manner: Ambiguum Clymene precibus Phaëthontis an irā Mota magis, it being uncertain whether, etc., (so, incertum, : dubium,).—
Of discourse, obscure, dark, ambiguous: scriptum,: verba ambigua distinximus,: oracula,: responsa,: divinatio,.—Subst.: ambĭgŭum, i, n., an obscure, dark saying: ambiguorum complura sunt genera,; ; Auct. ad ; : voces,.—
Trop., uncertain, wavering; not to be relied on, untrustworthy. —So of moral conduct: esse ambiguā fide,: puer acris ingenii sed ambigui,: femina bonis atque honestis moribus, non ambiguā pudicitiā,: per ambiguas vias,: domum timet ambiguam Tyriosque bilinguis,.—Of fortune, changing, fluctuating: ambiguarum rerum sciens, .!*? In Tac. with gen.: ambiguus imperandi,irresolute,: pudoris ac metus,wavering between shame and fear,: futuri,.—Adv.: ambĭguē, doubtfully, ambiguously, ; ; : pugnare,with doubtful success,

la:verb:ambio.gloss: to round, go round, pass around, skirt
senses: to round, go round, pass around, skirt
to solicit for votes, campaign, canvass
to strive to get something from somebody, seek, strive for
la:verb:ambio.html:
amb-ĭo, īvi, and ii, ītum, 4,
v. n. and a. (although from the root eo, it is regularly conjugated throughout; hence part. perf. ambītus; but ambitio and 2. ambĭtus follow the quantity of the simple verb, eo, ĭtum; in the imperf. ambiebat; also ambibat,; cf. P.; Zumpt, Gram. § 215).
Lit.: aliquid, to go round or about a thing (syn. circumeo): ut terram lunae cursus proxime ambiret,: ambibat Siculae cautus fundamina terrae,: jubet urbem ambiri,.—
Transf.
To surround, encircle, encompass (syn.: circumdo, cingo): insula, quam amnis Euphrates ambiebat,: ambitae litora terrae,: Thracam nec purior ambiat Hebrus,; (cf. : flumina campos cingentia; v. ambitus, I.): funiculus ambiebat gyrum ejus,: muros praealtum mare ambiebat,; so ; ; : (clipei) oras ambiit auro,: ambiente (gemmam) circulo coloris aurei,: Judam suo ambiebat exercitu,.—
T. t. to designate the manner in which candidates for office sought to procure votes (v. ambitio), to go round after, to solicit, canvass for votes (syn. peto): virtute ambire oportet, non fautoribus,: quod si comitia placet in senatu habere, petamus, ambiamus,: ambiuntur, rogantur,; : singulos ex senatu ambiundo nitebantur, ne etc.,.—With acc. of the office: magistratum sibi,.—
In gen., to solicit one for something, for his favor, friendship, etc., to strive for, seek to gain (syn.: peto, sector): qui ambīssent palmam histrionibus,: nisi senis amicos oras, ambis, * : reginam ambire affatu,: conubiis ambire Latinum,: te pauper ambit sollicitā prece Ruris colonus,: ambiebat Jason summum sacerdotium,.—With ut or ne: ambienti, ut legibus solveretur,: ambirent multi, ne filias in sortem darent,.—With inf.: donec ultro ambiretur consulatum accipere,: pauci, qui ob nobilitatem plurimis nuptiis ambiuntur,.
la:verb:ambio.inflection: īvi, and ii, ītum, 4, v. n. and a.

la:verb:ambeo.gloss: to round, go round, pass around, skirt

Lost, iv. 3; Haml. i. 4).—So of other things: Tristior illā Terra sub ambobus non jacet ulla polis,: Atridas Priamumque, et saevum ambobus Achillen,angry with both parties,.—
In gen., of two objects and no more, the two, both: QVOM. PERORANT. AMBO. PRAESENTES. (i.e. actor et reus), Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. : consules, alter ambove, si eis videretur,: ambo accusandi estis,: jam hisce ambo, et servos et era, frustra sunt duo,: erroris ambo complebo,: emit hosce ambos,: ut eos ambos fallam,; so : hic, qui utrumque probat, ambobus debuit uti,: una salus ambobus erit,: plebiscitis cautum, ne quis duos magistratus uno anno gereret, utique liceret consules ambos plebeios creari,: Caesar atque Pompeius diversa sibi ambo consilia capiunt ... eodemque die uterque eorum ex castris exercitum educunt,: amborum verba,: civitate Romanā ambos donavit,: ambo occisi,: errant autem ambo senes,; : applicuit ambos ad eum,; .—
Poet. = duo: partīs ubi se via findit in ambas,into two,.

la:verb:amburo.html:
amb-ūro, ussi, ustum, 3, v. a.,
to burn around, to scorch (opp. exurere, to burn entirely up); also, with an extension of the idea, to burn wholly up, to consume (most freq. in part. perf.; class.).
Lit.
Hadrianus vivus exustus est: Verres sociorum ambustus incendio, tamen ex illā flammā periculoque evasit,: Herculis corpus ambustum,: terret ambustus Phaëthon avaras spes,—So Cicero jestingly calls the tribune of the people Munacius Plancus, at whose suggestion the enraged populace set fire to the senate-house, tribunus ambustus, the singed tribune of the people, Moeb.—Of those whom the lightning had struck, but not killed: : tot circa me jactis fulminibus quasi ambustus,; so ; : Cassius, quem fama est esse libris Ambustum propriis,: magna vis frumenti ambusta,: ambustum theatrum,—Hence, ambu-stum, i, n., in medic. lang., a burn: inflammatio recentis ambusti,: sedare ambusta,: ambusta sanare,: ambusta igne vel frigore,—
From the similarity of effect, to injure by cold, to nip, benumb (cf. aduro): ambusti multorum artus vi frigoris,: ambusta pruinis lumina, i. e. oculi,.—
Trop.
Of property: ambustas fortunarum mearum reliquias,the charred remains,.—
Of one who, when tried for an offence, comes off with great trouble: qui damnatione collegae et suā prope ambustus evaserat,had come off scorched,.

ambiguus
,

la:verb:ambigo.html:
amb-ĭgo, ĕre (
perf. tense not used), v. n.
ago
.
Lit., to go about or around: ambigens patriam et declinans,,

15 fin.—

Trop., to wander about; to waver, hesitate, be undecided, to doubt, be in suspense (syn. dubito; class., but mostly in prose).—In this sense in Cic. either impers. or pass.
Impers.: Quale quid sit, ambigitur,is uncertain,: omnis res eandem habet naturam ambigendi, de quā disceptari potest,i. e. admits of arguments for and against,: ambigitur, quotiens uter utro sit prior,: de nomine ipso ambigi video,: adspici aliquando eam volucrem, non ambigitur,it cannot be doubted,.—
Personal: cui rei primum occurreret, ambigebat,: Alexandrum regnum Asiae occupaturum haud ambigere,; : causa, de quā tu ambigis,: ambigebant de illis,.—
Pass.: ambigitur status, in quo etc.,: in eo jure, quod ambigitur inter peritissimos,of which there is a doubt,; : in eis causis, quae propter scriptum ambiguntur,.—
Transf.
To argue, debate about something: ut inter eos, qui ambigunt, conveniat, quid sit id, de quo agatur,: ambigere de vero,.—
To contend, dispute, wrangle, etc.: vicini nostri ambigunt de finibus, * : ambigunt agnati cum eo, qui est heres,: de fundo,: de hereditate,: de regno,.

ambĭtus, ūs, m.

Lit.A going round, a moving round about, a revolution: cum se octo ambitus ad idem caput rettulerint,: aquae per amoenos ambitus agros, (cf. ambio, II. A.): alligata mutuo ambitu (i. e. amplexu) corpora,: ambitu breviore luna currit quam sol,: saeculorum,: verborum (i. e. ambages),.—
Transf.
Abstr. pro concr., a circuit, circle, circumference, periphery, edge of a circular object: ambitus parmae,: folia ambitu serrato,: castra lato ambitu,; : ambitus lacus,.—Trop., of discourse, periphrasis, circumlocution, = ambages: multos circa unam rem ambitus facere,.—Hence, the open space left round a house: ambitus est quod circumeundo teritur, Müll.: P. Scaevola id solum esse ambitus aedium dixerit, quo etc.,: ambitus proprie dicitur inter vicinorum aedificia locus duorum pedum et semipedis ad circumeundi facultatem relictus, Paul. ex Müll. —Also, the small space around sepulchres, .—
An unlawful striving for posts of honor, or canvassing for office; esp. by bribery (cf. ambitio, I.), prohibited by the Lex Calpurnia, Caecilia, Fabia, Julia, Licinia, Tullia de ambitu, against bribery, corruption, etc.: legem ambitus flagitāsti,: punire ambitum,; cf. Kritz: accusare aliquem ambitus,: deferre nomen alicujus de ambitu,: interrogare aliquem legibus ambitus,: damnatus ambitus,: condemnare de ambitu,: effusae ambitus largitiones,.—
In gen., the desire to make a display, ostentation, vanity, show, parade: relinque ambitum: tumida res est vana, ventosa,: proprius quidam intellegendi ambitus,.—Of speech, bombastic fulness, parade: imagine et ambitu rerum, Fr.; —
In rhet., a period: comprehensio et ambitus ille verborum (si sic periodum appellari placet),; ; so .
